title: Mini Review: Resident Evil 2 Deluxe Edition (Switch 2) - Finally Gets The Treatment It Deserves
summary:
RPD-elightful.

Capcom’s decision to release a bunch of modern Resident Evil games on the Switch via the cloud was controversial, to say the least. While I personally had a pretty positive experience with Resident Evil 2 - Cloud Version, it wasn't an ideal solution for RE fans on Switch. Thankfully, with the release of RE2 Deluxe Edition on Switch 2, we finally have a native version of a modern classic, and it’s brilliant.

In case you missed Capcom’s 2026 Switch 2 releases, the company has demonstrated mastery of Nintendo’s hardware, delivering games that look incredible and run well. That’s exactly the case here, too. Resident Evil 2 looks amazing, with sharp, clear visuals in both docked and handheld modes. Really, the only obvious drawback is the slight fuzziness of character hair, which is a lot more noticeable when playing handheld.

title: Mini Review: Resident Evil 3 (Switch 2) - An Impressive Port Of A Subpar Remake
summary:
Stars don't shine.

It’s generally accepted that Resident Evil 3 is the worst of the series’ modern remakes. While RE2 and 4 both expanded upon their respective originals, RE3 made several cutbacks to environmental design, campaign structure, and the behaviour of the main antagonist, Nemesis.

The result is an undeniably disappointing experience, but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth playing. There’s still a lot to like here as you’re funnelled through the five-to-six-hour story at breakneck pace, but it’s just a shame that it’s now Jill-sandwiched between two much more accomplished entries. Still, I’m thankful that it’s now available natively on Switch 2 after Capcom’s subpar Cloud Version in 2022.

title: Review: Resident Evil 4 Gold Edition (Switch 2) - The Gold Standard For Remakes
summary:
Leon top form.

The original Resident Evil 4 is one of my favourite games of all time – if not my number one. I remember soaking in every detail before its release, with magazines chronicling its troubled development alongside Capcom’s shaky promise of GameCube exclusivity. When it launched in 2005, it devoured my every waking moment for the rest of the year, and I still regularly play it.

For a long time, I was of the opinion that it simply didn’t need a remake. It still looks good, it plays great, and I couldn’t imagine how Capcom could possibly do it justice. When my older brother, however, picked up the original for the first time a few years back, he dropped it almost immediately, repulsed by the ageing controls and mechanics. Was I wrong?

title: Review: Ratatan (Switch 2) - Patapon-Style Rhythm-Action Strategy Returns, With A Roguelite Twist
summary:
Ratamatazz.

Released at the height of the rhythm-action boom and following the march of peripheral-based music games, Patapon was a visually unique treat. The result of a collaboration between game designer Hiroyuki Kotani and French artist Rolito Giuli, this curio had you control a tribe of tiny eyeball creatures by tapping out rhythms on face buttons.

The original game and its sequel received a Switch release last year, and it was a perfect fit for the console, given the series' roots on Sony's beloved PSP. Now Kotani returns with Ratatan, a crowdfunded spiritual successor that ramps up the madness and adds a roguelite spin.

summary:
Here come the grannies!

Following an impressive entry from Halfbrick with Bluey’s Quest for the Gold Pen, developer Gameloft is taking a crack at the beloved IP with Bluey’s Happy Snaps. After Gold Pen's more fantastical approach, this latest adventure brings things back to basics, making for a charming, lighthearted experience that kids will absolutely enjoy.

title: Mini Review: Resident Evil 3 (Switch 2) - An Impressive Port Of A Subpar Remake
summary:
Stars don't shine.

It’s generally accepted that Resident Evil 3 is the worst of the series’ modern remakes. While RE2 and 4 both expanded upon their respective originals, RE3 made several cutbacks to environmental design, campaign structure, and the behaviour of the main antagonist, Nemesis.

The result is an undeniably disappointing experience, but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth playing. There’s still a lot to like here as you’re funnelled through the five-to-six-hour story at breakneck pace, but it’s just a shame that it’s now Jill-sandwiched between two much more accomplished entries. Still, I’m thankful that it’s now available natively on Switch 2 after Capcom’s subpar Cloud Version in 2022.

summary:
Leon top form.

When it launched in 2005, it devoured my every waking moment for the rest of the year, and I still regularly play it.

summary:
Ratamatazz.

Released at the height of the rhythm-action boom and following the march of peripheral-based music games, Patapon was a visually unique treat. The result of a collaboration between game designer Hiroyuki Kotani and French artist Rolito Giuli, this curio had you control a tribe of tiny eyeball creatures by tapping out rhythms on face buttons.

The original game and its sequel received a Switch release last year, and it was a perfect fit for the console, given the series' roots on Sony's beloved PSP. Now Kotani returns with Ratatan, a crowdfunded spiritual successor that ramps up the madness and adds a roguelite spin.

That's a lot of Rings.

Earlier this year, SEGA revealed a life-size Sonic statue that contained the hedgehog's "DNA" (yes, really), housed in the Shibuya SEGA store. In the months since, a trip to Tokyo has been the only way you could get a look at the weird creation, but you'll soon be able to have one in your home... if you can stomach the insane price tag.

As brought to our attention by Dexerto, the "DNA"-filled statue will soon be available as a smaller figurine for an eye-watering ¥3,300,000 (which is around $20,000 or £16,000, for those wondering). It's now available to pre-order from the Kadokawa store and is expected to ship (oh yes, the above cost doesn't include shipping) in January 2027 — not that it matters, because who is buying this??

title: Nintendo States That It Has No Plans To Ditch Physical Media
summary:
"We know how much the fans like it".

Bill van Zyll, vice president and general manager of Nintendo Latin America, has stated that the company currently has "no plans to ditch physical" media.

This comes via an interview with Coelho no Japão on YouTube (thanks Nintendo Everything) at a time in which physical media is more at risk than ever. With Sony confirming its plan to cease production of PlayStation discs in early 2028 and Microsoft likely to follow suit, questions have no undoubtedly lingered as to whether Nintendo will also go all-digital. Thankfully, that doesn't seem to be the case... at least for now.

title: Feature: How Do You Pronounce These Words From Zelda: Ocarina Of Time?
summary:
Sheikdown.

The upcoming return to 64-bit Hyrule has us discussing Ocarina of Time memories, chatting about our favourite characters and bosses, and generally looking wistfully into the middle distance with a smile on our faces, wondering how all these people and places will look in reimagined form on Switch 2.

In the course of these chats, however, we've found that we don't all say these people's names in quite the same way. We've investigated Pokémon and more general Nintendo-related words before, but not Ocarina specifically. There's only one way to say 'Ocarina', right?

title: Feature: Box Art Brawl - Duel: Wii Sports Resort
summary:
Which is the Wuhu winner?

Hey everyone! Welcome to this week's edition of Box Art Brawl!

Last time, we matched up a trio of covers for the GBA's Zone Of The Enders: The Fist Of Mars, though it wasn't a particularly close-fought contest. The Japanese variant walked away with 54% of the vote and the win, leaving the European and North American designs with 29% and 17% respectively.
